purpose: Bounded randomized support episode from Medicaid consumer-directed allowance to informal-caregiver wellbeing and financial-strain outcomes, preserving care-recipient, household, durability, and cultural-response gaps.

events.geography: United States; Arkansas, Florida, and New Jersey Medicaid demonstration
events.date_precision: study-period reference date; beneficiaries were randomized after baseline interviews and primary informal caregivers were interviewed about 10 months later across state-specific field periods
events.denominator: Primary informal caregivers identified by participating beneficiaries at baseline; published state caregiver interview counts were 1,433 Arkansas, 1,193 Florida, and 1,042 New Jersey
events.method: HHS/ASPE report using the Cash and Counseling randomized design, beneficiary-identified primary caregiver baseline information, and caregiver follow-up interviews
events.missingness: Caregiver task hours, exact paid amount, recipient clinical outcome, employment/earnings, household buffers, provider alternatives, long-run persistence, trust, collective action, and exit are not retained in this compact record
events.exposure: A Medicaid beneficiary with a primary informal caregiver was randomized to consumer-directed Cash and Counseling support or usual personal-care/home-and-community-based services
events.alternatives_before_action: Usual services, consumer-directed hiring, other family help, paid replacement, respite, and non-use were possible routes; the compact record does not observe each caregiver's feasible option set
events.immediate_burden_or_benefit: The consumer-directed allowance changed the service-control and payment route available to the beneficiary and caregiver
events.choice_or_response: Treatment beneficiaries could adjust service amount, timing, and type, hire the primary caregiver, name the caregiver as decision maker, or purchase assistive devices/home modifications
events.person_or_actor_with_control: The program and beneficiary controlled the allowance and service direction; caregivers could be hired or remain unpaid, while the recipient's needs and household alternatives constrained practical control
events.remedy_or_institutional_response: Medicaid consumer direction supplied a monthly allowance and counseling/support route in place of relying only on usual service delivery
events.remedy_receipt: Treatment assignment and caregiver follow-up are observed at study level; individual allowance receipt, spending, payment timing, and completed service use are not retained in this compact record
events.durability_followup: Caregiver outcomes were measured about 10 months later; longer-run care continuity, household security, recipient health, and recurrence remain open
events.immediate_outcome: Across the three states, treatment and paid-caregiver routes improved selected caregiver wellbeing, satisfaction, and perceived financial-strain measures relative to usual-service controls; effects were not uniform across every outcome
events.protected_outcome: Consumer direction could reduce caregiver strain, improve control over service timing/type, and make some caregivers' physical or emotional burden more manageable
events.sacrificed_outcome: Residual unpaid labor, care coordination, health risk, household time, and financial exposure may remain; the study does not establish that all burdens disappeared
events.cost_risk_transfer: Consumer direction can move control toward the beneficiary and caregiver, but it can also leave service coordination and care risk inside the household
events.later_outcome: The report supplies a roughly 10-month caregiver follow-up but not long-run employment, earnings, recipient safety/health, care continuity, trust, political action, or exit
events.meaning_and_attribution: Caregiver satisfaction and perceived strain are measured, but broader fairness, dignity, identity, blame, or institutional legitimacy are not retained as a cultural-response endpoint
events.public_or_collective_response: No collective or political response is measured
events.counterexample: A support program can improve caregiver wellbeing without proving restored caregiver employment, complete recipient recovery, or elimination of unpaid care
events.source_and_uncertainty: HHS/ASPE, How Cash and Counseling Affects Informal Caregivers: Findings from Arkansas, Florida and New Jersey, 2005; randomized assignment supports treatment contrasts, but caregiver outcomes and state-specific implementation are study-bound

arrows.to: beneficiary/caregiver control over service amount, timing, and type
arrows.evidence: The ASPE report describes random assignment to Cash and Counseling or usual services and identifies the treatment mechanisms as hiring, decision-making, service adjustment, and assistive-device/home-modification purchase
arrows.counterexample: Assignment does not mean every beneficiary used the allowance or changed service use in the same way
arrows.remaining_gap: Individual take-up, spending, service use, payment timing, and care-plan completion

arrows.to: caregiver wellbeing and perceived financial-strain improvement
arrows.evidence: ASPE reports that treatment caregivers fared better than controls on at least half of 15 key wellbeing and satisfaction measures and that the intervention alleviated perceived financial strain in all three states
arrows.counterexample: Effects differed across outcomes and states; the intervention did not discernibly change caregiver household income
arrows.remaining_gap: Outcome-specific effect sizes, take-up, caregiver task intensity, and household resource mediation

arrows.evidence: The report states that paid treatment-group caregivers showed better outcomes than controls on important emotional-strain and physical-health measures, with effects generally larger than among unpaid treatment caregivers
arrows.counterexample: Payment may select or enable different care arrangements; the compact public result does not identify the mechanism or exact amount
arrows.remaining_gap: Paid hours, wage/allowance amount, care substitution, task reduction, and longer-term health/work outcomes

arrows.from: caregiver support and reduced perceived strain
arrows.to: care-recipient continuity, household security, and durable recovery
arrows.evidence: The caregiver follow-up measures caregiver outcomes, but the compact report does not join caregiver change to recipient clinical outcomes, household earnings, later care continuity, or long-run security
arrows.counterexample: Caregiver relief can coexist with unmet recipient need, new household costs, or later service loss
arrows.remaining_gap: Same beneficiary-caregiver pair, completed service, recipient safety/health, household resources, and persistence

arrows.to: trust, collective action, switching, or exit
arrows.evidence: The ASPE report does not measure institutional attribution, political response, collective organizing, provider switching, or care-route exit
arrows.counterexample: A recipient or caregiver may experience improved control without changing institutional trust or public behavior
arrows.remaining_gap: Meaning, legitimacy, action, provider choice, non-use, and exit

boundary: This ledger adds a randomized care-support-to-caregiver-wellbeing segment. It does not establish that every beneficiary or caregiver took up the allowance, that recipient care was completed or adequate, or that household recovery, trust, action, or exit followed.
storage_boundary: Only the public ASPE report's study-level design, sample counts, and bounded outcome statements are retained; no beneficiary, caregiver, Medicaid, or claims microdata are stored.
